en: The Definition of Valid Cognition.
Homage to the venerable gurus. Hariḥ Oṃ.
Having prostrated before Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of lords, the teacher of all without exception, who is free from all affliction, I shall explain the specific definitions of the means of valid cognition.

Valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which corresponds to reality. It is of two kinds: direct perception (*kevala*) and inference (*anumāna*). Direct perception is knowledge that corresponds to reality; the means for attaining that is inference. Direct perception is fourfold.
[The manifestation of Śiva] occurs through the distinction between Īśvara, Lakṣmī, and the yogin.
The first two [categories] are beginningless and eternal. Their specific difference [from one another] is due to independence (*svātantrya*) and dependence (*pāratantrya*).
The former [Īśvara] has as its object all particularities residing in both himself and others.
The second [type] belongs to Īśvara; it is superior to that of others.

It is not universal; elsewhere, it pertains to all objects. There is a distinction regarding clarity. The knowledge of yogis is constant for the upright, but for Īśvara, it is superior to that of individual souls (jīvas).
Elsewhere, in the case of mere observation (*ālocana*), it pertains to all objects, increasing sequentially until liberation; thereafter, it is immutable.
Prior to that, it decreases sequentially; and elsewhere than in the case of the ultimate principles (*tattva*), it has a beginning.

The knowledge of one who is not a yogi possesses arising and destruction; it is limited. Valid cognition (*anupramāṇa*) is threefold: perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and scripture (*āgama*).
Perception is the contact of the sense organs with an object that is free from defects.
Valid origination from a faultless source is inference (*anumāna*). Faultless verbal testimony is scripture (*āgama*).
Presumption (*arthāpatti*) and analogy (*upamā*) are specific forms of inference.
Non-existence (*abhāva*) is both inference and perception.
[The determination of meaning] arises from the distinction between apprehension and non-apprehension; it consists of the inference of possibility (*saṃbhava*) and elimination (*pariśeṣa*).

The inference of defects includes self-dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), circularity (*cakraka*), infinite regress (*anavasthā*), conceptual complexity (*kalpanāgaurava*), and the abandonment of what is heard or seen in scripture. Furthermore, there are the six marks of scriptural interpretation: the opening statement (*upakrama*), the concluding statement (*upasaṃhāra*), uniformity (*tadaikarūpya*), repetition (*abhyāsa*), novelty (*apūrvatā*), the result (*phala*), and explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).
The distinctions of origin;
those very origins together with their logical grounds (*liṅga*);
the name (*samākhyā*), as well as syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), and position (*sthāna*); and the specific logical grounds (*liṅgaviśeṣa*).
Pervasion (*vyāpti*) is rooted in logical justification (*upapatti*). It takes the form of the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
The proposition may contain the reason within itself, or it may be stated alone; likewise, when the proposition is established, the mere reason suffices.
The example may be accompanied by the proposition or contain the reason within itself. Logical justification consists of consistency (*virodha*) and non-contradiction (*asaṅgati*).
In matters of what is prescribed by scripture, whether deficient or excessive, points of defeat (*nigraha*) consist precisely in the failure to state the correspondence [of one's position].
Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is of seven kinds: that of the witness (*sākṣi*) and the six types of sense organs; recollection (*smṛti*) arises from mental direct perception.
There is no lack of authority in restatement and subsequent mention,
because they are experienced as being in accordance with reality and because there is no loss [of meaning].
There is contradiction [only] with respect to the Mantra and its own sentence.

Contradiction with one's own statement occurs in the form of an *apasiddhānta* (departure from a tenet) and a *jāti* (futile rejoinder). A *jāti* such as "the means of knowledge does not depend on the object of knowledge" is [invalidated] because, by that very same reasoning, it is established that the means of knowledge does indeed depend on the object of knowledge.

Furthermore, there is contradiction with human convention (*mānavirodha*), which constitutes a fallacy of equivocation (*chala*) and a lack of logical connection (*asaṅgati*). Moreover, as another example: when one says "bring the cow" intending a young cow (*gṛṣṭi*), it is impossible to bring a cow intending the earth (*pṛthivī*). Contradiction is threefold, distinguished by the categories of thesis (*pratijñā*), reason (*hetu*), and example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
A proposition whose meaning contradicts valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is a contradiction of the proposition (*pratijñāvirodha*).
The non-establishment of the nature of the reason (*hetu*) and its lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) constitute a contradiction of the reason (*hetuvirodha*).
The failure of the probandum (*sādhya*) or the probans (*sādhana*) to follow through in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is a contradiction of the example (*dṛṣṭāntavirodha*).
Only a contradiction of equal strength with the proposition constitutes a counter-proof (*sapratīsādhana*).

That very same thing is also the fault of a limiting condition (*upādhi*). All of these [faults] are to be seen in the inference of "visibility" (*dṛśyatva*), because the world's reality is established by perception, scripture, and so forth.
Because, on that view, the property of being visible (*dṛśyatva*) is false;
and because the opponent does not accept the existence of the indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*).
Regarding the phrase "of the indeterminable": this is because even the Self (*ātman*) is visible.
Because nacre-silver and the like lack indefinability;
because that which is indefinable lacks the property of being an object of perception;
and because [the reason] "because it is established by the mind" is subject to a counter-argument (sapratipakṣa).

If perception, which grasps the reality of the world, were restricted to grasping only the present moment, then—since there would be no distinction in its being a form of perception—the validity of inference and scripture, which grasp [objects] in subsequent moments, would not be established; consequently, only statements regarding difference (*bhedādi*) and so forth would possess validity.
If it is argued that the validity of that [perception] is established by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣi*), then the reality of the world is likewise established by the witness-consciousness.

If there is deviation [in the inference], then it is the same regarding the determination of the faultlessness of the meaning of the scripture and the inference. Consequently, on the following day, the meaning of a statement of non-difference would be difference; the faultless inference would become faulty, and the faulty inference would become faultless—thus, there is a lack of systematic consistency.

The fallacies of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), the probandum (*sādhyāsiddhi*), and the locus of the reason (*adhikaraṇāsiddhi*) are not genuine defects, because there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For it is only through over-extension that one would have to consider something a defect when it is not;
indeed, it is pervasion (*vyāpti*) alone that is the determining factor.
Even when [the subject] is non-existent, pervasion certainly exists. Furthermore, how can it be prevented—without relying on pervasion—that that which has a non-existent locus cannot be a prover?
If such qualifiers as "having an unreal substratum" and so forth are possible, how can there be a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*)?

Furthermore, even absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is not devoid of all attributes, because it is experienced as being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*), and because the authority of presumptive reasoning (*arthāpatti*) by way of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) is accepted. This is because, in the argument "the subject of dispute has a creator," the possession of omniscience is admitted as a necessary factor for the proof through the force of its being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).

The distinction [between presumption and inference] is merely this: presumption is the remainder, while inference is [the process of] logical necessity (*arthāpatti*); for both consist simply in a logical possibility (*upapatti*).
Furthermore, since logical possibility must in every respect be admitted to depend upon pervasion (*vyāpti*), the difference [between them] is based on mere insistence.
This is because even comparison (*upamāna*) possesses the nature of pervasion; for indeed, nothing dissimilar has ever been observed to be similar to itself.
And non-apprehension of the fit [object] is a logical mark (liṅga), because there is no distinction.
Because there is no distinction. Because there is no distinction. Because there is no distinction.
All defects of inference are included within the defects already mentioned.

That which is not distinct from the probandum is "unestablished" (asiddhi). That which establishes what is already established is "incoherent" (asaṅgati). A means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not that which produces valid cognition (*pramā*);
for there is no evidence for a valid cognition that is distinct from the act of knowing.
Nor is there any proof for the claim that valid cognition is merely the determination of an object previously unknown.
This is because validity (*prāmāṇya*) is accepted as being nothing other than correspondence with reality (*yāthārthya*).

Furthermore, experience (*anubhūti*) alone is not the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it would fail to apply (*avyāpti*) to memory (*smṛti*) and the like, and because the validity of the Vedas, inference (*anumāna*), and so forth is well-established. [As it is said: "Memory, perception (*pratyakṣa*), tradition (*aitihya*), and inference—these are the fourfold [means of knowledge]."

"It should be understood as a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa) by those desiring to exist for the sake of dharma and other goals," so says the Śruti. Furthermore, oral tradition (aitihya) is a variety of scripture (āgama). Nor is it the case that a means of valid knowledge is simply that which produces correct experience, because [such a definition] would fail to apply to the knowledge of the Lord (īśvara) and so forth.

Furthermore, there is the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding invalidity, as well as regarding the knowledge of validity. Even if that [knowledge of validity] were accepted, it would lead to an infinite regress.
And if a self-luminous nature (*svaprakāśātman*) were accepted, it would fail to apply to that [self-luminous nature itself].
Furthermore, if the validity of memory is not admitted, there would be a lack of any means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the cognition "this was experienced by me.

If its validity were instead established through inference (*liṅga*), there would be the fault of conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*) as well as the loss of what is directly perceived (*dṛṣṭa-hāni*).
Moreover, if one posits only two types of valid cognition—perception and inference—there would be a contradiction with experience, because such a view fails to exclude false cognition and the like.
If it is said that there is an absence of its experience, and if it is then asked what the answer is when it is stated that neither experience nor memory exists, [the reply is:

"Establishment is by means of what is established for oneself; refutation is by means of what is established for the other. Therefore, in a refutation, there is no such fault as *apasiddhānta* (deviation from one's own tenets).
An "admission of the desired" (*iṣṭāpatti*) is entirely irrelevant because it constitutes the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*).
By the sage Ānandatīrtha, following the path set forth in the *Brahmatarka*, the definition of valid cognition has been stated in brief for the sake of establishing Brahman.

Salutations to you, O Nārāyaṇa, the sole witness of all that is measured and all that is to be measured without exception, whose form is imperishable, who is unborn, the Lord, praised by the many-invoked Indra, and worthy of worship.
Thus ends the excellent treatise on the definition of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇalakṣaṇa*), composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
